howToRefresh: Ingest the KY History morning email to public/content/raw-briefs/YYYY-MM-DD.md, run npm run parse-briefs, then npm run build (includes build-home-preview). The homepage also re-reads stories.json in the browser.

stories.title: Peter Cartwright, the backwoods preacher from Logan County
stories.summary: Raised in Logan County when it was called Rogues’ Harbor, Peter Cartwright was converted at a sacramental meeting in 1801, licensed to exhort in 1802, and rode Methodist circuits for two decades before leaving slave-state Kentucky for Illinois in 1824.
stories.quote: Peter Cartwright grew up in the roughest corner of the Kentucky frontier and spent his long life preaching to people like the ones he knew there.

photo.title: Portrait of Peter Cartwright
photo.credit: Unknown photographer · New York Public Library (Pageant of America collection) · public domain

stories.heroDeck: Peter Cartwright grew up in the roughest corner of the Kentucky frontier and spent his long life preaching to people like the ones he knew there.

stories.title: Madisonville, a courthouse town on McGary and Silkwood land
stories.summary: Hopkins County was created on December 9, 1806, and in 1807 its seat was laid out on 40 acres given by Daniel McGary and Solomon Silkwood and named for Secretary of State James Madison.
stories.quote: Madisonville began with a gift of forty acres and a name borrowed from President Jefferson's cabinet.

photo.title: The Hopkins County Courthouse in Madisonville, with the Confederate monument on the courthouse lawn (photographed 2017)
photo.attribution: Jim.henderson · Wikimedia Commons · CC0

stories.heroDeck: Madisonville began with a gift of forty acres and a name borrowed from President Jefferson's cabinet.

stories.title: I. W. Bernheim, from peddler to I. W. Harper
stories.summary: Isaac W. Bernheim landed in New York in 1867 with about four dollars, peddled in Pennsylvania until his horse died, built Bernheim Brothers and the I. W. Harper label in Paducah and Louisville, and gave Kentucky Bernheim Forest.
stories.place: Bernheim Bros. on Main Street, Louisville
stories.quote: Isaac Wolfe Bernheim landed at Castle Garden, New York's immigrant station, at noon on April 8, 1867.

photo.title: Isaac W. Bernheim as a peddler in Pennsylvania, 1867, a plate in his The Story of the Bernheim Family (1910)
photo.attribution: Unknown photographer · The Story of the Bernheim Family (1910) · Internet Archive (University of Louisville) · public domain

stories.heroDeck: Isaac Wolfe Bernheim landed at Castle Garden, New York's immigrant station, at noon on April 8, 1867.

stories.title: Fort Jefferson, Clark's fort on Chickasaw ground
stories.summary: In April 1780 George Rogers Clark planted Fort Jefferson and the village of Clarksville near the mouth of the Ohio on Chickasaw land he never bought. A Chickasaw siege that August destroyed the corn, and Virginia gave up the post on June 8, 1781.
stories.quote: George Rogers Clark reached the mouth of the Ohio on April 19, 1780, and his Illinois Battalion began a stockade in what is now Ballard County.

photo.title: Looking south over the river bottoms of Ballard County (photographed 2018)
photo.attribution: Brian Stansberry · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0

stories.heroDeck: George Rogers Clark reached the mouth of the Ohio on April 19, 1780, and his Illinois Battalion began a stockade in what is now Ballard County.

stories.title: The Treaty of Lancaster, 1744: how Virginia claimed Kentucky
stories.summary: At Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in 1744 the Six Nations gave Virginia a deed to the lands of its colony for goods and £200 in gold. Virginia read it as reaching the Mississippi; the Iroquois said they had sold only to the Alleghenies.
stories.quote: The treaty made at Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 1744 was negotiated hundreds of miles from Kentucky, but it became one of the paper foundations of Virginia's claim to the land. ## A council in a courthouse From late June into early July 1744, about 250 Iroquois delegates led by Canassatego of the Onondaga met colonial commissioners in the court house at Lancaster.

photo.title: Title page of A Treaty, Held at the Town of Lancaster, in Pennsylvania … in June, 1744, printed and sold by B. Franklin, Philadelphia, 1744
photo.attribution: B. Franklin, printer · U.S. National Archives via DPLA · public domain

stories.heroDeck: The treaty made at Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 1744 was negotiated hundreds of miles from Kentucky, but it became one of the paper foundations of Virginia's claim to the land.

layers.name: Big Bone Lick
layers.blurb: A Pleistocene salt lick where mastodons left bones in the mud — Kentucky’s window on deep time.

photo.title: Big Bone Lick State Park
photo.attribution: Mattguyver · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 3.0

layers.name: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
layers.blurb: Flagship Kentucky Historical Society museum, covering more than 12,000 years of the Commonwealth.

photo.attribution: Lee Wright · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0

layers.name: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace
layers.wiki: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park
layers.blurb: The Sinking Spring farm where Lincoln was born in 1809, plus the Knob Creek boyhood unit.

photo.title: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace memorial
photo.attribution: Jon698 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0

layers.name: Blue Licks Battlefield
layers.wiki: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park
layers.blurb: August 19, 1782: the last major Revolutionary War battle in Kentucky.

photo.title: Blue Licks Battlefield monument
photo.attribution: Nyttend · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Old Talbott Tavern
layers.blurb: Court Square tavern since the late 1700s — among America’s oldest inns, still a working bourbon bar.

photo.attribution: Christopher L. Riley · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Goddard Covered Bridge
layers.blurb: White Bridge: a Town-lattice span over Sand Lick Creek, among Kentucky’s surviving covered bridges.

photo.attribution: Greg Hume · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Bourbon Iron Works
layers.blurb: Jacob Myers blew in a charcoal blast furnace here in 1791 — munitions for the early Commonwealth.

photo.title: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
photo.attribution: Jeff Bates · HABS / Library of Congress · Public domain

layers.name: The Kentucke Gazette
layers.blurb: Kentucky’s first newspaper, begun August 11, 1787 by John and Fielding Bradford.

photo.attribution: William Henry Perrin / Filson Club · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Cumberland Falls
layers.blurb: The “Niagara of the South,” and one of the few Western Hemisphere places a moonbow can appear.

photo.attribution: Aaron Vowels · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0

layers.name: Frankfort Cemetery
layers.blurb: Hilltop rural cemetery (1844) overlooking the capital — Daniel and Rebecca Boone were reinterred here.
